51: Keep blue at the upper edge as coral's temporary wall; bring coral home before releasing blue. An accessible hold-before-capture reminder, not a new movement rule.
52: Use coral as a vertical stopping wall for blue, then finish coral. Contrasts with 51's lateral approach and reversed first capture.
53: Move blue into the right-hand helper position before coral approaches; blue may go home once that stop has been used. First explicit relocated wall.
54: Approach the adjacent top-row helper from the right to land blue precisely; shortest, focused reverse-approach breathing room after relocation.
55: Hold blue one row above coral's target approach until coral has used the stop; preserve the useful resident instead of capturing immediately.
56: Relocate coral twice so blue can use perpendicular stops before either capture; one helper must serve two different launch lines.
57: Use coral's initial upper stop, then move coral to a lower row to stop blue again. Contrasts initial usefulness with deliberately rebuilt usefulness.
58: Exchange helper roles along the bottom row: coral first stops against blue, then blue needs coral's relocated position before blue can leave.
59: Reverse the same-row role exchange into a vertical left-edge problem: blue first depends on coral, then coral needs blue. Different approach/capture sequence from 58.
60: Prepare blue at the bottom-left for coral's vertical stop, then use coral's bottom-row position for blue's horizontal approach; reciprocal roles across two axes.
61: Bring the two residents into adjacent upper-row stopping positions before resolving neighboring interior goals; neither initial position is already useful.
62: Build an upper-left stop for blue, then keep blue at the upper-right to stop coral horizontally; turn a corner rather than repeat a straight handoff.
63: Move coral inward from the right edge for blue's lateral stop, then blue must return down the shared column before coral can continue. Contrasts 62's perimeter handoff with an interior return.
64: Blue needs coral below its start, then coral needs blue to its right; coral captures first, reversing the perpendicular exchange's release order.
65: Move away from the shared starting column to construct two adjacent bottom-row stops, then separate into interior destinations; a horizontal exchange with different exit geometry from 61.
66: Keep both residents alive through three role exchanges: coral uses blue on the left, blue uses coral above, and coral returns vertically to blue before captures can begin.
67: A three-resident relay on the right column: mint uses coral, blue uses mint, and coral uses blue; mint captures first without disconnecting the remaining pair.
68: Build a three-way dependency cycle across alternating axes; mint uses coral, coral uses blue, then blue still needs mint after coral has captured.
69: Cascade three residents into adjacent bottom-row stops, then coral still needs mint for its vertical exit after blue leaves; retain a late helper through the first capture.
70: Two-resident integration contrast: construct adjacent upper stops and then reuse blue vertically for coral. Unlike 66, the final approach is to neighboring upper goals rather than opposite interior goals.
71: Mint uses coral on the left, blue uses mint above, and mint needs coral again on the far right after blue captures; one helper must survive a long lateral relocation.
72: Trade places along the upper row through a three-resident relay, then release coral first while blue still depends on mint; avoid prematurely removing the middle helper.
73: Coral serves both blue and mint from the same right-column stop, then coral needs blue relocated to the left; a shared helper becoming a traveler, not three independent trips.
74: Start with blue's useful wall, then coral must relocate twice to furnish blue's lower and upper rightward stops. Repeated helper reuse rather than a three-piece cycle.
75: Mint traverses a row between coral's far-right stop and blue's left stop; coral then depends on mint between them. Bidirectional relay with coral released before mint and blue.
76: Mint uses relocated coral below and blue's initial position to its right; blue captures, but mint must remain as coral's final stopper. Teach why first capture need not release every helper.
77: Coral and mint exchange helper roles vertically, then mint needs blue on a perpendicular exit. Keep blue useful until the connected pair has completed its preparation.
78: Two-resident out-and-back contrast: coral crosses to blue's right-side wall, blue returns against coral, then blue relocates below coral's final approach. Interior exits distinguish it from the upper-edge setups in 66/70.
79: Use mint's initial bottom-row wall, then blue and coral complete a three-way row relay; mint captures first and the remaining pair still exchange roles.
80: Blue must survive while coral uses it twice at different heights and mint stops against coral in between; capture coral and mint before the indispensable blue helper.
81: Retain all three residents through five helper stops before any capture; the mostly vertical relay must end in a horizontal handoff, so immediate goal chasing destroys the setup.
82: Relocate every participant through a full dependency cycle and an additional return to the first helper; all four stops precede the first capture.
83: Blue's initial stop serves mint, mint then stops coral on two perpendicular approaches, and coral finally serves blue; reuse a moving helper across axes before releasing it.
84: Start from mint's useful initial wall, exchange coral/mint roles across two axes, then make blue help mint before coral can use mint again; a connected branch feeding back into the first pair.
85: Mint initially helps coral; coral must then help mint twice, and mint still helps blue after coral leaves. One pair's preparation has to preserve a third resident's late route.
86: Coral and mint exchange roles three times before the first capture; mint must remain for blue's final stop even after coral is safely home.
87: Blue's initial wall starts mint's route; blue and mint trade perpendicular helper roles, then mint must remain for coral after blue captures. Resolve the late branch without losing its stopper.
88: Mint's initial wall serves both coral and blue; the other two then exchange helper roles across axes before mint may capture last. Shared resource followed by reciprocal preparation.
89: Relocate mint to blue, reverse their roles across axes, then coral needs both of them at different stages including a stop after blue captures. A two-helper finish rather than a simple chain.
90: Keep mint initially useful to blue and coral, then coral alternates between newly positioned blue and mint; blue returns against coral, and mint still needs coral after blue captures.
91: Coral helps blue initially, blue then helps mint, and coral's original stop must remain available to mint; blue still needs relocated mint after coral captures.
92: Blue needs mint, mint needs coral, then blue needs coral and mint on different axes; hold all residents through the four-stop preparation before the first capture.
93: Mint first uses coral's initial wall; blue uses mint next, then coral depends on blue before and mint after blue's capture. The final traveler needs two different helpers across alternating axes.
94: Use coral's initial wall to prepare blue, then blue serves both other residents at different heights; blue returns against coral, coral uses mint, and mint still needs blue after coral captures. Six-stop branching cycle with blue released last.
95: Mint uses coral initially, blue uses mint, and blue's relocated lower wall must serve both mint and coral before blue captures. Shared late wall is prepared by an earlier reciprocal exchange.
96: Capstone: coral's initial wall starts blue, then blue and mint must repeatedly rebuild adjacent upper stops through a long return loop; mint still needs coral on a perpendicular exit after blue captures. Coral must remain until last.
97: Capstone: relocate coral to serve mint vertically and blue horizontally; mint then serves blue's upward approach twice, with blue serving coral between those visits. A cross-axis hub-and-return sequence, all prepared before the first capture.
98: Capstone: assemble three adjacent bottom-row stops through a cyclic relay, then mint must use relocated blue horizontally and coral vertically before anyone can leave. The lower-row cascade feeds a two-helper upper exit.
99: Capstone: blue and mint trade lower vertical stops, but mint must subsequently use coral above and blue to the right; coral can then capture while blue still needs mint below. A long setup that releases a third-party helper before the reciprocal pair.
100: Regional finale: mint first needs relocated coral below, coral needs blue above and mint below, then blue needs coral for its own intermediate stop. After coral captures, mint still needs blue at the upper stop. Keep blue out of its tempting lower nest until mint is home, then release blue last.
